en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.1 (SN 5.1, SN 162, PTS [1st ed. SN i 128, PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 281) 1. Bhikkhunīvagga Āḷavikāsutta (The Discourse to Āḷavikā)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā dressed, took her bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after her meal and returning from her almsround, she approached the Blind Men’s Grove seeking seclusion.

Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā and wishing to drive her away from seclusion, approached the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā; having approached, [he addressed] Āḷavikā...
He addressed the bhikkhunī with a verse:
“There is no escape in the world;
what will you achieve by seclusion?”
“Enjoy the delights of sensual pleasure;
do not be one who regrets it later.
Then, this thought occurred to the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā:
“Who is this, whether human or non-human, who speaks this verse?
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā:
“This is Māra the Evil One; desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in me, and wishing to drive me away from seclusion, he speaks this verse.”
Then the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā, knowing, “This is Māra the Evil One,” replied to Māra the Evil One in verses:
“There is an escape from the world,
well-touched by my wisdom;”
O Evil One, friend of the heedless,
you do not know that state.
Sensual pleasures are like spears and spikes.
The hammering down of the aggregates;
that which you call delight in sensual pleasures has become a source of displeasure for me.”
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The bhikkhunī Āḷavikā knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya 5.2 (SN 5.2, SN 163, PTS [1st ed. SN i 129; PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 283) 1. Bhikkhunīvagga*
The Somā Sutta.
The setting was Sāvatthī.
Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Somā dressed, took her bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after his meal and returning from his almsround, he approached the Blind Men’s Grove for his midday rest.
Having entered the Blind Men’s Grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and terror of the hair standing on end in the bhikkhunī Somā, [approached her].
Desiring to cause her to fall away from concentration, he approached the bhikkhunī Somā; having approached, he addressed the bhikkhunī Somā with a verse:
"That state which is to be attained by seers, so difficult to realize—"
“That cannot be attained by a woman with the wisdom of two fingers.
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Somā:
“Who indeed is this, a human or a non-human, who recites this verse?
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Somā:
“This is Māra the Evil One; desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in me, and wishing to cause me to fall away from concentration, he recites this verse.”
Then the bhikkhunī Somā, knowing, “This is Māra the Evil One,” replied to Māra the Evil One with verses:
“What can the female state do,
when the mind is well-composed?
While knowledge is present for one who correctly discerns the Dhamma—
surely for such a person this would be so:
"Whether it be 'I am a woman' or 'I am a man,' or anything else whatsoever—
Māra is not fit to speak such things."
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, "The bhikkhunī Somā knows me," being pained and dejected, vanished right there.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.3 (SN 5.3, SN 164, PTS [1st ed. SN i 129; PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 284) 1. Bhikkhunīvagga*
The Kisāgotamī Sutta.
The setting was Sāvatthī.
Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī dressed herself, took her bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after her meal and returning from her almsround, she approached the Blind Men’s Grove;
having approached it, she sat down at the foot of a certain tree for her midday rest.
Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and horripilation in the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī, [approached her].
Desiring to cause her to fall away from concentration, he approached the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī;
having approached, he addressed the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī in verse:
“Why do you look like one whose son has died?”
“Alone for a month, with tears on your face, you have come into the middle of the forest;
are you perhaps searching for a man?”
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī:
“Who is this, a human or a non-human, who speaks this verse?
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī:
“This is Māra the Evil One, who wishes to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in me, and who wishes to cause me to fall from concentration; he speaks this verse.
Then the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī, knowing, “This is Māra the Evil One,” replied to Māra the Evil One in verses:
“I am one whose son is utterly dead;”
For men, this is the end;
I do not grieve, I do not weep,
nor do I fear that, friend.
Delight is destroyed everywhere;
the mass of darkness is shattered;
having conquered the army of Death, [I stand].
“I dwell free from taints.
Then Māra the Evil One, realizing, “The bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.4 (SN 5.4, SN 165, PTS [1st ed. SN i 130, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 286)*
1. Bhikkhunīvagga.
Vijayāsutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Vijayā dressed herself...
[and] sat at the foot of a certain tree for her midday rest.
Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in the bhikkhunī Vijayā, said this:
Desiring to cause her to fall away from concentration, he approached the bhikkhunī Vijayā;
having approached, he addressed the bhikkhunī Vijayā with a verse:
“You are young and beautiful...”
"And I am young and vigorous;
come, noble sir, let us delight ourselves with the fivefold musical ensemble."
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Vijayā:
“Who is this, a human or a non-human, who recites this verse?
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Vijayā:
“This is Māra the Evil One; wishing to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in me, and wishing to cause me to fall from concentration, he speaks this verse.
Then the bhikkhunī Vijayā, knowing, “This is Māra the Evil One,” replied to Māra the Evil One in verses:
“Forms, sounds, tastes, and smells...”
And delightful tactile objects—
I offer these to you alone,
Māra; I have no need for them.
Because of this putrid body,
fragile and subject to breaking,
I am distressed and ashamed.
Craving for sensual pleasures has been uprooted.
So too for those beings who have reached the realm of form,
and those who abide in the formless realm.
“And that peaceful attainment—
everywhere darkness has been dispelled.
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The bhikkhunī Vijayā knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.5 (SN 5.5, SN 166, PTS [1st ed. SN i 131, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 287) 1. Bhikkhunīvagga The Discourse on Uppalavaṇṇā At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhunīs: “Bhikkhunīs, come hither. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhunīs replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhunīs, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a blue lotus; the person who is like a red lotus; the person who is like a white lotus; and the person who is like a fragrant lotus. And how, bhikkhunīs, is one a person like a blue lotus? Here, bhikkhunīs, a bhikkhunī is virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and having undertaken the training rules, she trains herself in them. This is her virtue. She experiences the bliss free from sensual pleasures and free from unwholesome states that belongs to the first jhāna, which is secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, and which is born of seclusion. This is her concentration. She possesses wisdom regarding the arising and passing away of phenomena, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This is her wisdom. Just as a blue lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water—so too, bhikkhunīs, a bhikkhunī is virtuous... [as before] ...she possesses wisdom. This is called a bhikkhunī who is like a blue lotus. And how, bhikkhunīs, is one a person like a red lotus? Here, bhikkhunīs, a bhikkhunī is virtuous... [as before] ...she possesses wisdom. She experiences the bliss free from directed thought and evaluation that belongs to the second jhāna, which is the internal refinement and single-pointedness of mind, devoid of directed thought and evaluation, and which is born of concentration. This is her concentration. She possesses wisdom regarding the arising and passing away of phenomena... [as before] ...leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This is her wisdom. Just as a red lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, remains at the same level as the water—so too, bhikkhunīs, a bhikkhunī is virtuous... [as before] ...she possesses wisdom. This is called a bhikkhunī who is like a red lotus. And how, bhikkhunīs, is one a person like a white lotus? Here, bhikkhunīs, a bhikkhunī is virtuous... [as before] ...she possesses wisdom. She experiences the bliss of equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, which belongs to the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: ‘He dwells happily, mindful and equanimous. This is her concentration. She possesses wisdom regarding the arising and passing away of phenomena... [as before] ...leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This is her wisdom. Just as a white lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water—so too, bhikkhunīs, a bhikkhunī is virtuous... [as before] ...she possesses wisdom. This is called a bhikkhunī who is like a white lotus. And how, bhikkhunīs, is one a person like a fragrant lotus? Here, bhikkhunīs, a bhikkhunī is virtuous... [as before] ...she possesses wisdom. She experiences the state of the cessation of perception and feeling, having attained it through the complete stilling of perception and feeling. This is her concentration. She possesses wisdom regarding the arising and passing away of phenomena... [as before] ...leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This is her wisdom.

Just as a fragrant lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water—so too, bhikkhunīs, a bhikkhunī is virtuous... [as before] ...she possesses wisdom. This is called a bhikkhunī who is like a fragrant lotus. These, bhikkhunīs, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer, the Teacher, further said this: “The blue lotus, the red lotus, The white lotus, and the fragrant lotus— These are the four kinds of persons Found existing in the world. The one who is like a blue lotus Is virtuous and of good conduct; Having abandoned sensual pleasures, She attains the first jhāna. The one who is like a red lotus Is virtuous and of good conduct; Having stilled directed thought and evaluation, She attains the second jhāna. The one who is like a white lotus Is virtuous and of good conduct; Experiencing equanimity and mindfulness, She attains the third jhāna. The one who is like a fragrant lotus Is virtuous and of good conduct; Having attained the cessation of perception and feeling, She dwells in peace, having reached the goal. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhunīs delighted in the Blessed One’s words. (This concludes the fifth discourse in the Bhikkhunīvagga.)
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā dressed herself...
[and] stood at the foot of a certain sāla tree that was in full bloom.
Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and horripilation in the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā,
and wishing to cause her to fall away from concentration, approached the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā; having approached,
he addressed the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā with a verse:
“O Bhikkhunī, having approached the supreme flowering tree,
you stand alone at the foot of the sāla;
there is no second element of beauty for you.”
“O foolish girl, do you not fear rogues?
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā:
“Who is this, a human or a non-human, who speaks this verse?”
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā:
“This is Māra the Evil One; desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in me, and wishing to cause me to fall from concentration, he speaks this verse.
Then the bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā, having recognized, “This is Māra the Evil One,” replied to Māra the Evil One in verses:
“Even if hundreds of thousands of such rogues were to come here,
I would not quiver nor tremble with fear.”
I am not afraid of you, O Māra, even though I am alone.
I shall either vanish from sight or enter into your belly.
Even in the space between the ribs,
you will not see me standing there;
for I have attained mastery over the mind.
The bases of psychic power have been well developed;
I am freed from all bonds,
friend, and I do not fear.”
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The bhikkhunī Uppalavaṇṇā knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 5.6 (SN 5.6, SN 167, PTS [1st ed. SN i 132; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 290) 1. Bhikkhunīvagga (The Chapter on Bhikkhunīs)
The Cālā Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Cālā dressed herself... [and so on].
He sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Then Māra the Evil One approached the bhikkhunī Cālā; having approached, he said this to the bhikkhunī Cālā:
“Bhikkhunī, what is it that you do not find pleasing?”
“I do not approve of birth, friend.
“But why do you not approve of birth?
One who is born experiences sensual pleasures.”
"Who indeed has incited you to this?
O bhikkhunī, do not delight in birth.
"For one who is born, death occurs."
Once born, one encounters sufferings:
bondage, slaughter, and affliction;
therefore, I do not delight in birth.
The Buddha taught the Dhamma for the transcendence of birth and for the abandoning of all suffering.
He established me in truth:
those beings who have reached the realm of form,
and those who dwell in the formless realm;
“Not understanding cessation,
they return to renewed existence.
Then Māra the Evil One, realizing, “The bhikkhunī Cālā knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.7 (SN 5.7, SN 168, PTS [1st ed. SN i 133, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 291) 1. Bhikkhunīvagga Upacālāsutta At Sāvatthī. Then the bhikkhunī Upacālā approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “It is not easy, Upacālā, for one who has not seen this Dhamma to know the Dhamma in brief, or to live practicing in accordance with that Dhamma, unless one has developed a strong inclination toward it, cultivated it, made it a vehicle, made it a basis, established it, and mastered it. “But, venerable sir, how much of the Dhamma must one have developed... mastered, so that one could know the Dhamma in brief, or live practicing in accordance with that Dhamma? “Suppose, Upacālā, a king had a frontier city with strong ramparts, walls, and arches, and with six gates. The gatekeeper there was wise, competent, and intelligent; he would not allow those who were enemies or foes to enter, but would allow those who were friends and well-wishers to enter. Now, Upacālā, suppose people from the east, having prepared a great caravan, would approach that city from the eastern direction, and they would ask the gatekeeper: ‘Where, friend, is the king’s frontier city with strong ramparts, walls, and arches, and with six gates? The gatekeeper would point out the city to them: ‘Just beyond this grove, friends, is the king’s frontier city with strong ramparts, walls, and arches, and with six gates. Then those people, having entered the city through the eastern gate, would explore it thoroughly, and having explored it, they would exit through the western gate. Having exited, they would ask the gatekeeper: ‘Friend, what is the name of this city? ‘Friends, this is the king’s frontier city named “Endowed with Six Gates. Then those people, having prepared another great caravan, would approach that city from the southern direction... the western direction... the northern direction... the northeastern direction... the southeastern direction... the northwestern direction, and they would ask the gatekeeper: ‘Where, friend, is the king’s frontier city with strong ramparts, walls, and arches, and with six gates? The gatekeeper would point out the city to them: ‘Just beyond this grove, friends, is the king’s frontier city with strong ramparts, walls, and arches, and with six gates. Then those people, having entered the city through the northeastern gate, would explore it thoroughly, and having explored it, they would exit through the southwestern gate. Having exited, they would ask the gatekeeper: ‘Friend, what is the name of this city? ‘Friends, this is the king’s frontier city named “Endowed with Six Gates. In the same way, Upacālā, suppose a bhikkhu is endowed with faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. He would think: ‘I have developed the path, but I do not know whether I have fully realized the fruit of the path. Then, having gone to a forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, he should sit down cross-legged, keeping his body erect and establishing mindfulness before him. As he sits, he should reflect: ‘Is there within me any lust for the form element? If, while reflecting, he knows: ‘There is no lust for the form element within me,’ then he should further reflect: ‘Has the fruit of the path been realized by me? If, while reflecting, he knows: ‘The fruit of the path has been realized by me,’ then he has known the Dhamma in brief and lives practicing in accordance with that Dhamma. If, while reflecting, he does not know: ‘There is no lust for the form element within me,’ then he should further reflect: ‘Have I not developed the path? If, while reflecting, he knows: ‘I have not developed the path,’ then he should apply himself to its development. If, while reflecting, he knows: ‘There is lust for the form element within me,’ then he should further reflect: ‘What is the cause and condition for this lust? He should understand: ‘This lust arises because of unwise attention and because of non-restraint of the sense faculties. Then he should practice wise attention and exercise restraint over the sense faculties. By practicing wise attention and exercising restraint over the sense faculties, that lust will be abandoned and will not arise in the future. He should reflect: ‘Is there within me any lust for the feeling element? ... ‘Is there within me any lust for the perception element? ... ‘Is there within me any lust for the volitional formations element? ... ‘Is there within me any lust for the consciousness element? If, while reflecting, he knows: ‘There is no lust for the consciousness element within me,’ then he should further reflect: ‘Has the fruit of the path been realized by me? If, while reflecting, he knows: ‘The fruit of the path has been realized by me,’ then he has known the Dhamma in brief and lives practicing in accordance with that Dhamma. If, while reflecting, he does not know: ‘There is no lust for the consciousness element within me,’ then he should further reflect: ‘Have I not developed the path? If, while reflecting, he knows: ‘I have not developed the path,’ then he should apply himself to its development. If, while reflecting, he knows: ‘There is lust for the consciousness element within me,’ then he should further reflect: ‘What is the cause and condition for this lust? He should understand:

‘This lust arises because of unwise attention and because of non-restraint of the sense faculties. Then he should practice wise attention and exercise restraint over the sense faculties. By practicing wise attention and exercising restraint over the sense faculties, that lust will be abandoned and will not arise in the future. It is in this way, Upacālā, that a bhikkhu has known the Dhamma in brief and lives practicing in accordance with that Dhamma. When this was said, the bhikkhunī Upacālā said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way the Blessed One has explained the Dhamma in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. “Upacālā, women do not easily gain full confidence in a teacher even after a long time, nor in the Dhamma, nor in the Saṅgha. But since you have gained full confidence in the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, it is fitting for you to exert yourself in order to abandon the five lower fetters. “Yes, venerable sir,” the bhikkhunī Upacālā replied. Then she rose from her seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to her right, and departed. Not long after the bhikkhunī Upacālā had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, the bhikkhunī Upacālā is wise. If she had applied herself to the abandoning of the five lower fetters, she would have become one of the non-returners, or one of the once-returners, or one of the stream-enterers. But since she has gained full confidence in the Teacher, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, it is fitting for her to exert herself in order to abandon the five lower fetters. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir! those bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, he is capable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. What five? Here, a bhikkhu is possessed of faith, virtuous, learned, generous, and wise. When a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is capable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the bhikkhunī Upacālā, having dressed in the morning time... [and so forth]...
sat down at the foot of a certain tree for her midday rest.
Then Māra the Evil One approached the bhikkhunī Upacālā; having approached, he said this to the bhikkhunī Upacālā:
“Where, bhikkhunī, do you wish to be reborn?
“I do not wish to be reborn anywhere at all, friend.”
“The Tāvatiṃsa gods, the Yāma gods,
and also the Tusita deities;
the Nimmānarati gods, [and the Paranimmitavasavatti gods].”
“To those gods who are the Vasavattīs,
direct your mind there;
you shall experience delight.”
“The Tāvatiṃsa gods, the Yāma gods,
and also the Tusita deities;
the Nimmānarati gods, and the Paranimmitavasavatti gods.”
Those gods who are subject to the Vasus and are bound by the fetters of sensual desire,
they again fall under the power of Māra.
The entire world is ablaze;
the entire world is smoldering;
the entire world is aflame.
The entire world trembled.
It was unshakable, ablaze,
and not frequented by ordinary people.
“Where there is no path for Māra,
there my mind delights.
Then Māra the Evil One, realizing, “The bhikkhunī Upacālā knows me,” sorrowful and dejected, vanished right then and there.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.8 (SN 5.8, SN 169, PTS [1st ed. SN i 133, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 292) 1. Bhikkhunīvagga Sīsupacālāsutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the bhikkhunī Sīsupacālā approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, how many things, when developed and cultivated, lead to Nibbāna in this very life? “There are these four things, bhikkhunī, which, when developed and cultivated, lead to Nibbāna in this very life. What four? (1) Mindfulness of the body, bhikkhunī, when developed and cultivated, leads to Nibbāna in this very life. (2) Loving-kindness, bhikkhunī, when developed and cultivated, leads to Nibbāna in this very life. (3) The perception of impermanence, bhikkhunī, when developed and cultivated, leads to Nibbāna in this very life. (4) The perception of non-self in what is impermanent, bhikkhunī, when developed and cultivated, leads to Nibbāna in this very life. These four things, bhikkhunī, when developed and cultivated, lead to Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, the bhikkhunī Sīsupacālā said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhunīs: “Bhikkhunīs, if anyone should say: ‘I do not see even a single thing that, when developed and cultivated, leads to Nibbāna in this very life,’ that would be a false statement on his part. Or if he should say: ‘I do not see even a single thing that, when developed and cultivated, leads to Nibbāna in this very life,’ that too would be a false statement on his part. For there are these four things, bhikkhunīs, which, when developed and cultivated, lead to Nibbāna in this very life. What four? Mindfulness of the body, bhikkhunīs, when developed and cultivated, leads to Nibbāna in this very life. Loving-kindness, bhikkhunīs, when developed and cultivated, leads to Nibbāna in this very life. The perception of impermanence, bhikkhunīs, when developed and cultivated, leads to Nibbāna in this very life. The perception of non-self in what is impermanent, bhikkhunīs, when developed and cultivated, leads to Nibbāna in this very life. These four things, bhikkhunīs, when developed and cultivated, lead to Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, the bhikkhunī Sīsupacālā said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Sīsupacālā dressed herself... [and so on] ...
and sat down at the foot of a certain tree for her midday rest.
Then Māra the Evil One approached the bhikkhunī Sīsupacālā; having approached, he said this to the bhikkhunī Sīsupacālā:
“Bhikkhunī, whose sect do you approve of?
“I do not approve of anyone’s sect, friend,” she replied.
“With whom do you have in mind that you have shaved your head?
You appear like a female ascetic,
yet you do not approve of any religious sect.”
"Why do you wander about so deluded? [He replied:
"Those who are outside this [teaching], the heretics, place their faith in various views."
I do not approve of their doctrine;
they are unskilled in the Dhamma.
There is one born in the Sakya clan, who—
The Buddha is peerless;
he is the conqueror of all, the dispeller of Māra,
undefeated in every respect.
Liberated in every respect and unattached,
the one with vision sees all;
having reached the destruction of all karma, he is free.
Liberated through the destruction of the acquisitions;
he is my Blessed One, the Teacher,
and I delight in his teaching.
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The bhikkhunī Sīsupacālā knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.9 (SN 5.9, SN 170, PTS [1st ed. SN i 134; PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 294) 1. Bhikkhunīvagga*
The Selā Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Selā dressed herself … [as before] … and set out for the park.
He sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in the bhikkhunī Selā,
approached her and addressed the bhikkhunī Selā in verse:
“Who made this constructed image?
Where indeed is the maker of the image?
Where has the image arisen?”
“Where, then, does the reflection cease?
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Selā:
“Who is this, a human or a non-human, who speaks this verse?”
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Selā:
“This is Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, terror, and horripilation in me, and wishing to displace me from concentration, that he speaks this verse.
Then the bhikkhunī Selā, knowing “This is Māra the Evil One,” replied to Māra the Evil One in verses:
“This puppet is not made by itself,
nor is this suffering made by another;
it has arisen dependent upon a cause.”
Through the destruction of its cause, it ceases.
Just as a certain seed,
when sown in a field, grows forth.
Depending upon the essence of earth and moisture— both of these—
so too are the aggregates and the elements.
And these six sense bases have arisen in dependence upon a cause;
with the breaking up of that cause, they cease.
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The bhikkhunī Selā knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.10 (SN 5.10, SN 171, PTS [1st ed. SN i 134, PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 296) 1. Bhikkhunīvagga*
The Vajirā Sutta.
The setting was Sāvatthī.
Then, in the morning, the bhikkhunī Vajirā dressed, took her bowl and robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after his meal and returning from his almsround, he went to the Blind Men’s Grove for his midday rest.
Having entered the Blind Men’s Grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Then Māra the Evil One, desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and horripilation in the bhikkhunī Vajirā, approached her.
Desiring to cause her to fall away from concentration, he approached the bhikkhunī Vajirā;
having approached, he addressed the bhikkhunī Vajirā with a verse:
"By whom was this being fashioned?"
Where is the maker of a being?
Where has the being arisen?
And where does the being cease?
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Vajirā:
"Who is this, a human or a non-human, who speaks this verse?
Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Vajirā:
“This is Māra the Evil One, who speaks this verse desiring to arouse fear, trepidation, and horripilation in me, and wishing to cause me to fall away from concentration.
Then the bhikkhunī Vajirā, knowing, “This is Māra the Evil One,” replied to Māra the Evil One in verses:
“Why do you conceive of a ‘being’? ... [and so on] ...”
Māra, have you fallen into a false view?
This is merely a heap of conditioned formations;
herein no being is to be found.
Just as, through the combination of its parts,
there comes to be the designation "chariot," so too,
when the aggregates exist, [there is the designation "being"].
"The term 'a being' is a mere convention.
For it is only suffering that arises,
suffering that stands, and suffering that passes away."
“Nothing other than suffering arises;
nothing other than suffering ceases.
Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The bhikkhunī Vajirā knows me,” being pained and dejected, vanished right there.
